reframing_when: The question is being analyzed through a single disciplinary lens when the situation sits at the intersection of multiple domains — the frame is locked to one model when a lattice of models would reveal cross-domain structure.
The question keeps producing the same class of answers because the same mental model is being applied repeatedly — the model is a hammer and every problem looks like a nail.
The question treats its own framing methodology as transparent rather than as one of many possible lenses — the meta-question 'which models am I using to frame this?' has not been asked.

The question would benefit from triangulation — applying 2-3 models from different disciplines and seeing where they agree and where they conflict, using disagreement as a signal about the problem's structure.
reframing_move: Before settling on one analytical frame, ask: 'What would this problem look like through 2-3 models from entirely different disciplines, and where do those models disagree about what matters?' — the latticework reframe uses cross-model disagreement as a structural signal.
curation_note: Latticework of Mental Models (Munger) is a meta-reframing model — it insists on applying multiple models from different disciplines. The source describes 'building a broad toolkit of mental models from many disciplines', 'using multiple models to triangulate', and Munger's warning against 'the man with a hammer'. The scope_lock challenge is direct: single-discipline framing is the target. The habitual_frame challenge maps to Munger's hammer metaphor. Medium confidence because this is a meta-model (about using models) rather than a direct reframing tool, but its activation is genuine when single-lens framing is detected.

reframing_when.note: Single lens (multi-disciplinary toolkit concept), hammer problem (Munger's warning), transparent methodology (which models am I using?), triangulation (cross-model agreement/disagreement).

frame_patterns_challenged.note: Scope lock: single discipline constrains the frame. Habitual frame: 'man with a hammer' applies the same model. Borrowed premise: one model's assumptions become the premise. Option space collapse: one lens narrows options.
